title: Multiplication: groups, arrays and the area model

prompts: Draw 5 × 4 as equal groups and as an array. Write it as repeated addition.
Use an area model to work out 36 × 7. Show the two partial products.

pedagogy.rationale: One product is seen as groups, an array, a grid and repeated addition before the area model splits larger factors by place value.

prerequisiteAssumptions: Counts in equal steps (skip-counting by 2, 3, 5 and 10).
Knows the place value of tens and ones.

misconceptions.description: Adds the two numbers instead of multiplying them (4 × 3 = 7).
misconceptions.response: Draw the groups: 4 groups of 3 is 3 + 3 + 3 + 3, not 4 + 3.

misconceptions.description: Treats the tens digit as ones in a partial product (20 × 4 written as 2 × 4 = 8).
misconceptions.response: Keep the value of each part: 20 × 4 is 80, the area of a 20 by 4 rectangle.

misconceptions.description: Multiplies only some parts of the split, or forgets to add the partial products.
misconceptions.response: Every section of the area model is part of the whole rectangle: find each one, then add them all.

scenes.title: Bags of oranges
scenes.learnerAction: Look at the bags and think of a quick way to count the oranges.

content.body:
At the market, Ma Kumba has 4 bags with 3 oranges in each bag. You could count every orange, or you could use multiplication.

Today you will see one multiplication in four ways, then use a picture called an area model to multiply bigger numbers.

accessibility.textAlternative: Four bags with 3 oranges in each bag: 4 equal groups of 3, which is 12 oranges.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Read the scene, then press Continue.

scenes.title: One product, four pictures
scenes.learnerAction: Switch between groups, an array and a grid, and change the numbers.

content.body:
$4 \times 3$ means 4 groups of 3. Line the groups up in rows and you get an **array**: 4 rows of 3. Fill the rows with squares and you get a **grid** with an area of 12 squares.

Every picture shows the same total, $3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12$.
keyPoints: Equal groups, an array and a grid all show $4 \times 3 = 12$.
Turning the array gives $3 \times 4$: the same 12.

accessibility.textAlternative: Four times three shown four ways: 4 groups of 3 dots; an array of 4 rows with 3 dots in each; a grid of 4 rows of 3 squares with an area of 12 squares; and repeated addition, 3 plus 3 plus 3 plus 3 equals 12. Turning the array round shows 3 times 4, also 12.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Use the Groups, Array and Grid buttons, and the row and column sliders with the arrow keys.

blocks.caption: Multiplication is repeated addition of equal groups.

blocks.title: Turn it round
blocks.text: An array of 4 rows of 3 turned on its side is 3 rows of 4. So $4 \times 3 = 3 \times 4$.

visual.caption: Change the rows and columns. The groups, array, grid and repeated addition all update together.

scenes.title: Worked solution: chairs for assembly
scenes.learnerAction: Reveal each step of the worked solution.

content.body: Watch how the picture turns into a multiplication.

accessibility.textAlternative: The hall has 6 rows of chairs with 5 chairs in each row. That is 6 equal groups of 5, or 5 plus 5 plus 5 plus 5 plus 5 plus 5, which is 30 chairs. As a multiplication, 6 times 5 equals 30.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Press Show next step until every step is shown.

blocks.problem: The school hall has 6 rows of chairs with 5 chairs in each row. How many chairs are there?

steps.text: Find the equal groups: 6 rows, each with 5 chairs.
Write it as a multiplication: number of groups times the size of each group.
Check that the answer makes sense: 6 rows of 5 is more than 6 + 5 = 11, so 30 chairs is reasonable.

scenes.title: Solve with help: groups at the market
scenes.learnerAction: Turn equal groups into multiplications and calculate them, using hints if needed.

content.body: Find the equal groups, then multiply. Hints are here if you need them.

hints: Say it as groups: how many groups, and how many in each?

accessibility.textAlternative: Problem 1: 7 piles of mangoes with 4 mangoes in each pile; how many mangoes? Problem 2: a classroom has 5 rows of 8 desks; how many desks?
accessibility.keyboardPath: Tab to each answer box, type the number and press Check.

misconceptions.feedback: You added 7 + 4. There are 7 piles, each with 4: that is 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4.
You added 5 + 8. Each of the 5 rows has 8 desks: multiply.

hints: $5 \times 8$: count in eights five times, or in fives eight times.

scenes.title: Try it alone
scenes.learnerAction: Solve multiplications and match an array to its multiplication, without hints.

content.body: No hints this time. The solution appears after you check.

accessibility.textAlternative: Problem 1: 9 bundles of 6 sticks. Problem 2: 8 rows of 7 seedlings. Question: which multiplication matches an array of 3 rows with 5 dots in each row?
accessibility.keyboardPath: Tab to each answer box, type the number and press Check; choose one option for the question.

misconceptions.feedback: 15 is 9 + 6. There are 9 bundles of 6: multiply.

items.prompt: An array has 3 rows with 5 dots in each row. Which multiplication does it show?

options.feedback: Count the dots: each of the 3 rows has 5, so there are more than 8.
There are 3 rows, but each row has 5 dots, not 3.

scenes.title: Find the mistake: Kollie's oranges
scenes.learnerAction: Diagnose why an answer to 4 × 3 is wrong.

content.body: Kollie's answer is quick, but it does not match the picture. Find the mistake.

accessibility.textAlternative: Kollie said 4 bags of 3 oranges is 7 oranges, because 4 plus 3 is 7. He added the number of bags and the number in each bag. There are 4 groups of 3, which is 3 plus 3 plus 3 plus 3 equals 12.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Choose one option with the arrow keys and Space.

blocks.problem: Ma Kumba has 4 bags with 3 oranges in each bag. How many oranges?
blocks.question: What went wrong?

options.text: Kollie added the number of bags and the oranges in one bag.

options.feedback: Changing the order of an addition still gives 7. The problem needs equal groups added together.
Count the oranges in the picture: one bag alone has 3, and there are 4 bags.

correction: 4 bags of 3 is 4 equal groups of 3.

scenes.title: Split it: the area model
scenes.learnerAction: See a big multiplication split into easier parts by place value.

content.body:
Bigger numbers are easier in parts. $14 \times 6$ is a rectangle 14 long and 6 wide. Split the 14 into 10 and 4: you get two smaller rectangles, $10 \times 6$ and $4 \times 6$.

Add their areas to get the whole: $60 + 24 = 84$.

accessibility.textAlternative: Fourteen times six drawn as a rectangle 14 by 6, split into a 10 by 6 part and a 4 by 6 part. Ten times six is 60 and four times six is 24. Together, 60 plus 24 equals 84.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Read the model; nothing needs to be entered here.

blocks.caption: Split one factor by place value, multiply each part, then add.

scenes.title: Worked solution: two area models
scenes.learnerAction: Reveal each step of two area model solutions.

content.body: Watch one split, then a split of both numbers.

accessibility.textAlternative: Example 1: twenty-three times four. Split 23 into 20 and 3. Twenty times four is 80 and three times four is 12, so the answer is 92. Example 2: twenty-four times thirteen. Split both numbers: 20 plus 4, and 10 plus 3. The four parts are 200, 60, 40 and 12, which add to 312.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Press Show next step until every step of both examples is shown.

blocks.problem: A farmer plants 23 rows of cassava with 4 plants in each row. How many plants?

steps.text: Multiply each part by 4. Keep the value of the tens: $20 \times 4$ is 80, not 8.
Split both numbers: $24 = 20 + 4$ and $13 = 10 + 3$. That makes four rectangles.

scenes.title: Solve with help: fill the area model
scenes.learnerAction: Fill in each partial product and the total.

content.body: Fill in each part of the rectangle. The hint in the help panel shows where to start.

hints: Start with the tens: 10 × 7. Then the ones: 6 × 7. Then add.

accessibility.textAlternative: Sixteen times seven split into ten times seven and six times seven. Fill in 70 and 42, then add them to get 112.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Tab to each box in the model, type the product and press Check.

blocks.prompt: Work out $16 \times 7$ by filling in each part.

scenes.title: Try it alone: a bigger area model
scenes.learnerAction: Split both numbers and fill in four partial products without hints.

content.body: Both numbers are split this time. No hints: fill in every part, then the total.

accessibility.textAlternative: Twenty-five times twelve split into twenty plus five, and ten plus two. The four partial products are 200, 40, 50 and 10, which add to 300.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Tab to each box in the model, type the product and press Check.

scenes.title: Find the mistake: Sia's area model
scenes.learnerAction: Diagnose a mistake in a partial product.

content.body: Sia split the number correctly, but one part has the wrong value.

accessibility.textAlternative: Sia worked out twenty-three times four as two times four is 8, plus three times four is 12, giving 20. She treated the 2 tens as 2 ones. Twenty times four is 80, so the answer is 80 plus 12, which is 92.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Choose one option with the arrow keys and Space.

blocks.problem: Work out $23 \times 4$ with an area model.
blocks.question: What went wrong?

options.text: Sia used 2 instead of 20 in the first part.
options.feedback: Yes. The 2 in 23 means 2 tens. $20 \times 4 = 80$, so the answer is $80 + 12 = 92$.
Splitting 23 into 20 and 3 is a good start. The mistake comes after the split.

options.text: Sia should have multiplied 8 and 12 instead of adding.
options.feedback: The parts of an area model are added: they are pieces of one rectangle.

items.prompt: For $24 \times 13$, Musa found $200 + 12 = 212$. What did he miss?

options.feedback: Yes. Splitting both numbers makes four rectangles. Add all four: $200 + 60 + 40 + 12 = 312$.
Draw the rectangle: it has four sections, and Musa used only two of them.
There is no carrying here. Look at how many sections the rectangle has.

scenes.title: Apply it: supplies for the school
scenes.learnerAction: Solve two new real-world problems using any model you choose.

content.body: Choose a picture that helps: groups, an array or an area model. Then calculate.

accessibility.textAlternative: Problem 1: the school orders 18 boxes of chalk with 24 sticks in each box; how many sticks? Problem 2: the school farm has 15 rows of cassava with 13 plants in each row; how many plants?
accessibility.keyboardPath: Tab to each answer box, type the number and press Check.

blocks.prompt: Work out each total. Sketch an area model if it helps.

misconceptions.feedback: Check every part: $10 \times 20$, $10 \times 4$, $8 \times 20$ and $8 \times 4$. One part may be missing.
You found $10 \times 10 + 5 \times 3$ and missed two parts. Split both numbers and add all four pieces.

scenes.title: Remember
scenes.learnerAction: Recall the four pictures of multiplication and the area model steps.

content.body: Say each point aloud before the check.
keyPoints: Equal groups, arrays, grids and repeated addition all show the same product.
The area model splits a number by place value; keep the value of each part.
Find every partial product, then add them all.

accessibility.textAlternative: Equal groups, arrays, grids and repeated addition show the same product. The area model splits a number by place value; every partial product is found and added. A question asks for the partial products of 32 times 5: 150 and 10.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Choose one option with the arrow keys and Space.

options.feedback: $3 \times 5$ is 15, but the 3 in 32 means 3 tens: $30 \times 5 = 150$.
These come from adding. The parts of an area model are multiplied, then added.

scenes.title: Show what you know
scenes.learnerAction: Answer the assessment questions on your own.

content.body: Now show what you can do on your own. The assessment is checked by the assessment system, not by this lesson.

accessibility.textAlternative: The assessment asks you to represent and calculate multiplications on your own. It is delivered by the assessment player.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Answer each assessment question, then submit.

offline.note: Responses are kept until the device is online; the assessment authority scores them.
